core_principles.text: Spine-oriented verbal instructions can decrease spine flexion during lifting, specifically at intersegmental levels in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar regions.
Standard verbal cues to limit bending in the lower back may not be sufficient to target lower lumbar levels (L3/L4 to L5/S1), which are highly prone to injury and pain.
Developing a greater awareness of how to control and modify spinal posture can help individuals avoid irritating their backs during repetitive, prolonged, or loaded flexed postures.

common_mistakes.text: Lifting with a flexed spine, especially near the end range of motion, is a common technique error.
Performing repetitive flexion or flexing with a heavy load toward the end range of motion increases the risk of injury.

specific_findings.text: Following spine-oriented verbal instructions, maximum spine flexion angles significantly (p < 0.05) decreased at intersegmental levels in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar (T8/T9 to L2/L3) regions, but no significant changes were observed at the lower lumbar levels (L3/L4 to L5/S1).

consequences.text: Lifting with a flexed spine, especially near the end range of motion, increases the risk of low back injury and pain.
Repetitive flexion and flexing with a heavy load toward the end range of motion create high stresses on the posterior elements of the intervertebral disc, which can cause disc herniations.

In a flexed posture, the orientation of the erector spinae musculature changes so that their fibers align along the spine's compressive axis, impairing their ability to counteract anterior shear forces.
The anterior shear failure force of the spine is lower in a flexed posture compared to a neutral posture.

core_principles.text: Focusing on how much you round your lower back during lifts and consciously limiting the amount of rounding can reduce spine flexion.
The movement pattern chosen to avoid rounding the back should feel natural and not robotic or awkward.

common_mistakes.text: Regularly approaching maximum spine flexion during lifting.

specific_findings.text: In a pencil pick-up task, verbal instructions to limit lower back rounding significantly decreased the percentage of maximum flexion at T8/T9 (p = 0.0088, d = 1.2), T9/T10 (p = 0.0029, d = 1.2), T12/L1 (p = 0.0067, d = 1.0), and L1/L2 (p = 0.0149, d = 0.9).

In a free box lift task, verbal instructions to limit lower back rounding significantly decreased the percentage of maximum flexion at T8/T9 (p = 0.016, d = 1.0), T9/T10 (p = 0.012, d = 1.1), T11/T12 (p = 0.049, d = 0.8), T12/L1 (p = 0.0003, d = 1.4), L1/L2 (p = 0.0015, d = 1.2), and L2/L3 (p = 0.0471, d = 0.7).

In a box lift over a barrier task, verbal instructions to limit lower back rounding significantly decreased the percentage of maximum flexion in the gross lumbar region (p = 0.025, d = 0.9), L1/L2 (p = 0.017, d = 0.9), and L2/L3 (p = 0.031, d = 0.8).

Verbal instructions to limit lower back rounding did not produce statistically significant changes in the percentage of maximum flexion at the lower lumbar levels L3/L4, L4/L5, or L5/S1 across any of the tested lifting tasks (all p-values > 0.076).

consequences.text: Regularly approaching maximum spine flexion during lifting increases the risk of developing low back pain or injury.

core_principles.text: Verbal instructions alone can help reduce flexion at the lower thoracic and upper lumbar levels, but they are often insufficient for reducing flexion in the lower lumbar levels (L3-S1).
Applying regional tactile feedback, such as tape on the skin, can amplify proprioceptive input and successfully help a lifter reduce flexion across all lumbar intersegmental levels.
Allowing sufficient knee flexion during lifting tasks is essential to prevent forcing compensatory spine flexion to reach the ground.

common_mistakes.text: Failing to actively manage lower lumbar (L3-S1) flexion during lifting, as lifters naturally have poorer proprioceptive position sense in the sacral region compared to the upper spine.
Restricting knee flexion during a lift, which automatically forces the lifter to use greater spine flexion to reach down.

specific_findings.text: Without verbal instructions, participants consistently reached flexion angles exceeding 65% of their maximum range of motion in the lower lumbar intersegmental levels (L3-S1) during everyday lifting tasks.
Verbal instructions caused a significant decrease in absolute flexion angles at T8/T9 (p = 0.0002), T9/T10 (p = 0.0067), and T12/L1 (p = 0.0462) during a pencil-pickup task.
Verbal instructions significantly decreased absolute flexion angles in the gross lumbar region (p = 0.0281) and multiple intersegmental levels from T8 to L3 during a free-box lifting task.
When a barrier was used to limit knee flexion, verbal instructions failed to cause any significant changes in absolute spine flexion angles at any regional or intersegmental level.

core_principles.text: Instructions should not instill a fear of flexion-related movement, but rather should focus on developing an awareness of how spine flexion can be controlled under certain scenarios.
For individuals with a history of flexion-related pain or aggravation, teaching awareness of how they move their spines and how to reduce or control aggravating flexion can be beneficial.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing uncontrolled lumbar spine flexion during lifting tasks can increase the risk of low back pain or injury.

specific_findings.text: Verbal instructions designed to reduce spine flexion only resulted in statistically significant reductions in flexion at intersegmental levels at and above L2/L3, failing to significantly reduce flexion in the lower lumbar spine.

consequences.text: Lumbar spine flexion is a population-based risk factor for the development of low back pain or injury.
